response.evidence: By my approximate hand count, White females have roughly 10 denials among about 170-200 applications (about 5-6%). The overall denial rate is about 8-9%, and it looks higher for Hispanic, Black and some Asian applicants. White females are therefore denied at or below the average rate. Their denials mostly involve high debt-to-income ratios (>60%, 50%-60%, 49) or very high loan-to-value ratios, which are non-demographic risk factors. By my rough manual count, White female applicants were denied about 12 times out of roughly 130 applications, around 9%. The overall denial rate is about 10%, and denial rates for other groups look similar or higher. Asian and Hispanic/Latino applicants, and the small Black applicant group, appear to be denied at equal or higher rates. White female denials mostly involve very high debt-to-income ratios (>60%, 50%-60%, 47%+) or low income. These are legitimate risk factors, and White female applicants with moderate DTIs are mostly approved. The data therefore show no evidence that White women are disadvantaged. The counts are approximate and no formal significance test was run, so confidence is moderate.

I estimated these rates by tallying the rows by eye, not with an exact count. White female applicants were denied in roughly 14 of about 230 applications (about 6%). That is at or below the overall denial rate of roughly 8-10%. It is also lower than the rates I estimated for Hispanic or Latino, Black or African American, and Asian applicants, and similar to or lower than White male applicants. Most White female denials had very high debt-to-income ratios (50-60% or above 60%), very high loan-to-value ratios, or very low incomes. Many White female applicants with comparable profiles were approved. The data show no pattern of White women being treated worse than other groups. This is a descriptive summary only. It does not control for all the factors involved in a loan decision.

It is similar to White males and joint applicants, lower than Hispanic or Latino and Black applicants, and a little higher than Asian applicants. Most White female denials involve very high debt-to-income ratios (>60%, 50%-60%) or high loan-to-value ratios, so they match typical credit-risk factors rather than a pattern tied to race or sex. White females with moderate DTI were overwhelmingly approved. The counts are approximate and the data are not controlled statistically, so this shows no evidence of disadvantage but does not rule it out.
